listenings.text: Start at the market, and start at seven, because by ten it is a different place and by noon it is a photograph. Walk east from there, down the street that looks like nothing, past the two closed shops, and keep going for about fifteen minutes. You will come out at the cathedral square. Give it ten minutes. It is overrated, everybody who comes here sees it first, and it will tell you nothing you cannot get from a postcard. Then take the number four bus north for twenty stops. Get off when the buildings stop being interesting. Walk one residential street, slowly, and look at the balconies. That is the city. Nothing is happening there, and the fact that nothing is happening is exactly what you came to see.

Let me put the other side, and let me start by conceding most of it. Walkable cities are pleasant. The evidence on health, on street life, on the simple question of whether anybody talks to anybody, is real and I do not dispute it. My objection is narrower. In practice, in city after city, the schemes that make a district walkable also make it expensive, and within a decade the people the policy was written for cannot afford to live there. They now commute in, by car, from somewhere with no pavements at all. And here is the part that troubles me most. Those people are never in the room when the plan is drawn. The consultation happens where the residents are, and the residents of tomorrow are somewhere else entirely.

extra_audio.text: Clara says everybody who dislikes a city has spent two days in it, both in the centre. He concedes the point, noting that two days in the centre is what most visitors get. She replies that the centre is usually the worst part, teeming with visitors and abandoned by residents. He asks what she would send somebody to see instead of a guidebook gem. She answers with a market at seven and a residential street where nothing is happening.
